topics.name: Gravity
topics.kicker: Universal attractive force · Holds planets in orbit, keeps us on the ground
topics.dates: Formalized by Newton in 1687; reimagined by Einstein in 1915
topics.briefing: Gravity is the invisible pull that makes any two objects with mass attract each other, from a dropped pencil snapping to the floor to planets looping around the Sun. Isaac Newton described it as a universal force, while Albert Einstein later reimagined it as the curving of space and time itself. It is the weakest of nature’s four fundamental forces, yet it shapes the entire universe.

topics.name: Albert Einstein
topics.kicker: Physicist behind relativity · Rethought space, time, and gravity
topics.briefing: Albert Einstein was a German-born physicist whose theories of special and general relativity reshaped how scientists understand space, time, and gravity. His equation E = mc² showed that mass and energy are really the same thing, and his explanation of the photoelectric effect won him the 1921 Nobel Prize. He later emigrated to the United States and spent his final decades at Princeton.

topics.name: Friction
topics.kicker: Resistance between surfaces · Lets you walk, grip, and stop
topics.dates: Formally studied by Amontons starting in 1699
topics.briefing: Friction is the force that resists sliding when two surfaces rub against each other, whether it’s sneakers gripping a gym floor or a sled gliding over snow. It comes in a stronger static form, which must be overcome before motion starts, and a weaker kinetic form, which acts once something is already moving. Engineers fight it with lubricants like oil, while rock climbers and race car tires rely on it to grip.

topics.name: Mass
topics.kicker: Physics quantity · How much matter an object contains
topics.briefing: Mass is the simplest possible definition of “how much stuff” is packed into an object, measured in kilograms. It never changes no matter where an object travels, even though its weight does, since the Moon’s gravity pulls on the very same amount of matter far more weakly than Earth’s does. Albert Einstein’s famous equation even shows mass converting directly into pure energy.

trap.title: Mass, or weight?
trap.body: Real answer lines are explicit about this: several tossups on this quantity say “do not accept weight,” and a separate real tossup whose answer is weight itself says “do not accept mass.” The two are related but different: this quantity never changes no matter where an object goes, while weight is just the force of gravity pulling on it, and shrinks to about one-sixth of its Earth value on the Moon.
trap.fix: If the clue talks about gravity pulling on an object, a bathroom scale, or a value that changes between the Earth and the Moon, the answer is weight. If it describes how much matter is packed into an object, something that never changes no matter where it travels, give this quantity instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mass (do not accept weight; prompt on m)

topics.name: Acceleration
topics.kicker: Physics quantity · How fast velocity itself is changing
topics.dates: SI unit: meters per second, per second
topics.briefing: Acceleration measures how quickly something’s velocity is changing, whether it is speeding up, slowing down, or simply turning a corner at a constant speed. Isaac Newton’s second law ties it directly to force and mass: push twice as hard on the same object, and it accelerates twice as fast. Every object in free fall near Earth’s surface accelerates downward at the same rate, about 9.8 meters per second every second.

trap.title: Not velocity, and not force
trap.body: This quantity is easy to confuse with velocity or speed, since all three describe motion, but velocity can stay large and constant while this quantity is zero, and this quantity can be large even when velocity is momentarily zero, like at the top of a ball’s toss. It is also tempting to blurt out “force” when a question describes a push or a pull, but Newton’s second law makes clear that force and this quantity are related by mass, not identical to each other.
trap.fix: If the clue is about how fast something is moving, the answer is velocity or speed. If the clue describes a push or pull itself, the answer is force. Save this quantity for clues about how quickly velocity itself is changing — speeding up, slowing down, or turning.

topics.name: Frequency
topics.kicker: Physics quantity · How many repeats happen every second
topics.briefing: Frequency counts how many times something repeats every second, from the vibrations in a guitar string to the oscillations of a light wave, and it is measured in hertz. It is the mathematical reciprocal of a wave’s period, so a higher frequency always means a shorter period between repeats. A photon’s energy depends directly on its frequency, which is why gamma rays carry far more punch than radio waves.

trap.body: This quantity and the period are flip sides of the very same wave: multiply one by the other and the answer is exactly 1, so a question that gives the period and asks what it is the reciprocal of wants this quantity, not the period itself. topics.briefing: Inertia is matter’s built-in stubbornness: an object at rest stays at rest, and one in motion keeps moving in a straight line at a constant speed, unless an outside force pushes or pulls on it. Isaac Newton made this his First Law of Motion, building on Galileo’s idea that a ball would roll forever on a frictionless surface. It’s also why yanking a tablecloth fast enough can leave the dishes sitting still, and why more mass always means more resistance to changing speed.

trap.title: Inertia, mass, or moment?
trap.body: Mass and inertia are closely linked but not identical: mass is the numerical measure of how much inertia an object has, so a question built entirely around a formula, a unit, or a numeric value usually wants “mass” instead. “Moment of inertia” is a related but distinct rotational quantity, measured in kilogram-meters-squared, and its real answer line explicitly refuses the bare word “inertia.”
trap.fix: If the clues mention torque, angular acceleration, or a shape-dependent spinning quantity, the sharper answer is “moment of inertia,” not plain inertia. If the clues give a formula or a unit like kilograms, the answer is probably “mass.” Save “inertia” for clues about Newton’s First Law, reference frames, and the general tendency to resist changes in motion.

topics.kicker: Energy of motion · Equals one-half mass times velocity squared
topics.dates: Modern one-half-mv-squared formula settled in the 1800s
topics.briefing: Kinetic energy is the energy any moving object carries, from a thrown baseball to a speeding car, found with the formula one-half mass times velocity squared. Pull a roller coaster to the top of a hill and it’s loaded with stored, potential energy; let it go, and that energy converts into this kind as the cars race downhill. It’s conserved completely in a bouncy, elastic collision, but partly lost to heat and sound when a collision is inelastic.

topics.name: Black Holes
topics.kicker: Collapsed stars with inescapable gravity · Nothing, not even light, gets out
topics.dates: Predicted by general relativity, 1916; first imaged 2019
topics.briefing: A black hole is what’s left when a massive star collapses in on itself so completely that its gravity traps even light. Cross its boundary, called the event horizon, and nothing can ever climb back out. Despite that, physicist Stephen Hawking predicted these objects slowly leak radiation and shrink over time, and in 2019 astronomers captured the first-ever image of one, glowing at the center of a distant galaxy.

Unlike most forces, the strong force between them actually gets weaker at very short distances, a property called asymptotic freedom
The CKM matrix describes how these particles “mix” between flavors through the weak force
Briefly existed as a free, soup-like “plasma” with gluons for roughly the first ten microseconds after the Big Bang
Murray Gell-Mann borrowed their everyday name from a nonsense word in James Joyce’s novel _Finnegans Wake_
The heaviest “top” type was not confirmed until 1995, by teams at Fermilab’s Tevatron collider
An exotic bound state made of five of these particles was found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015
Thought to be the only known elementary particles that interact through all four fundamental forces, including gravity
An earlier classification scheme called the “Eightfold Way,” from physicists Murray Gell-Mann and Yuval Ne’eman, led to the fuller model
A 1974 discovery nicknamed the “November Revolution,” credited to Burton Richter and Samuel Ting, confirmed a heavier “charm” type

trap.title: Quarks, or electrons?
trap.body: Both are fundamental particles smaller than an atom, but they belong to different families. Electrons are leptons and are never affected by the strong force, so they never combine to form protons, neutrons, or any other particle built from the strong force. These particles, by contrast, are held together by the strong force (carried by gluons) and combine in threes to build every proton and neutron.
trap.fix: If the clues mention the strong force, gluons, color charge, confinement, protons, or neutrons, they want this answer. If the clues mention orbiting the nucleus, electric current, or the lightest charged particle, they want electrons instead.
